liarCellCount.paragraph: For the record, the liar cells file is settled. My note gave the data two doors: poison, or a rounding error, and it picked the second. A liar barely moves the clock. The study covered ten study days from April 22 to June 28, and the cost fell between 0% and about 3% per ten liar cells, which is thin either way. The best files are the ones I can stop writing in.

clueShare2.paragraph: In two study days, the answer for twos remained the same, with a range that puts it slightly above my hypothesis that a two should read almost as fast as a one. The range has narrowed by 29% since July 18. Each extra two in ten numbers adds about 5%, likely between 3% and 7%. The same answer repeated, and I am listening to the data.

clueShare4.paragraph: Every fresh look at fours gives the same reading, with the data showing that each extra four in ten numbers adds about 13% to your time, likely between 7% and 19%. This range has barely moved since Jul 18, with the number reading the same and the file staying open a while longer. My note asked how big the four costs, not whether it exists, and now the focus is on telling the fours apart from the boards around them.

patternMoves.paragraph: Back into the pattern reasoning file, I found that the number I left there isn't the same as the one I now have. The parked estimate moved significantly: from about 11% per ten pattern deductions on Jul 13, it now reads 43%. The cost associated with these deductions comes to about 43% per ten pattern deductions. The band estimate ranges from 35% to 53%. I wrote that a practiced read should cost seconds, not tens of seconds, and the data agree: the effect is real but small. I don’t like surprises in closed drawers.

sonarCellCount.paragraph: I closed the sonar file, and the parked estimate moved from about 37% per ten sonar cells on Jul 2 to 102% now. The model places this estimate between 68% and 142%. A number that shifts on its own has my full attention.

wormholePairCount.paragraph: The wormholes band is widening when it should be narrowing, and this trend is stark: the width has increased by 894% in this window. Ten wormhole pairs add about 49% to your time, with a likely range between 24% and 78%. I predicted that splitting one number across two places would slow the reading down, and it does. I haven’t retracted the hypothesis, but it’s on notice. I continue to collect data.

mysteryCellCount.paragraph: I opened the mystery cells file expecting progress and found the opposite. The range has widened by 43% since Jul 2. I wrote that missing information has a price, and I measured it. The charge per ten mystery cells reads between 0% and about 4%. When the data surprise me, I take better notes.

compassCellCount.paragraph: The compass question remains open, where I left it. My current estimate is about 65% per ten compass cells, likely ranging between 38% and 99%. The range has not moved. I wrote that I couldn’t tell whether players read the arrow fast or stopped to puzzle over it, and so far, neither can the model. The file stays open, and so does the question.
